newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bertelsmann regrets pay TV problems.
newsitem.headline: Bertelsmann regrets pay TV problems.

text.p: German publishing and media giant Bertelsmann AG, reporting an 11 percent rise in profits, said Wednesday it regretted recent developments that caused it to slam the brakes on its effort to offer digital pay television.

Net profit in the business year to the end of June was 905 million marks ($600.5 million), up from 817 million ($542 million) the year before. But weakness in German consumer markets hit operating profits, which fell 8 percent to 1.53 billion marks ($1.02 billion).
Group sales rose 5 percent to 21.5 billion marks ($14.3 billion), driven by continued expansion in the United States and Japan.

"In the end it was a business year that we could be satisfied with, although it was somewhat difficult," Chairman Mark Woessner told a news conference. "Growth was unusually small for us because we did not make much progress in Germany."
Woessner said he expected a one billion mark ($664 million) rise in sales this year and slightly higher profits.

Bertelsmann's activities range from being the world's largest book publisher to CD ROM production, music production, television and multimedia. But the company failed in its foray into digital pay television.
Rival media mogul Leo Kirch dashed ahead, spending around $5 billion in Hollywood this year for movie rights and setting up his DF1 digital broadcaster in Germany.

Woessner said he regretted that Kirch drove prices for movies so high that the market no longer seemed to promise the profits once expected. He stressed that digital pay TV would remain only a small part of the total television market.
"It will never have the importance of free TV," he said.
BMG Entertainment, which groups the company's electronic media activities, posted the highest sales volume, with 8.6 billion marks ($5.7 billion), up 9 percent from a year ago.
BMG Chairman Michael Dornemann said the division would concentrate on expansion of the music business -- boasting stars like Whitney Houston, Toni Braxton and Ace of Base.
Gruner+Jahr, Germany's largest magazine publisher, which accounts for one-third of Bertelsmann's operating profit, had sales of 4.6 billion marks ($3.1 billion), up 4 percent.

Board member Thomas Middelhoff, in charge of corporate development and multimedia, said a European joint venture with America Online was growing much more quickly than expected and would have two million subscribers by the year 2000.
"AOL is approaching a period of strong growth in Europe parallel to its development in the United States over the past few years," he said.
While most of the company's business is in print media, Bertelsmann forecasts that 45 percent of its business will be in electronic media by the year 2000.
